title: Distributed Cache
prompt: Many teams cache database results in their own ad-hoc ways. Design a shared in-memory cache cluster for the whole company, handling 1.5 million reads per second, that survives node failures and never knocks over the databases behind it.

clarify.q: Is the cache only ever a copy of data held elsewhere, or will some data live only in the cache?
clarify.why: If every value can be rebuilt from a database, we can skip persistence and accept losing a node's contents. If not, it is really a database, and needs replication guarantees and durability.

clarify.q: How stale may a cached value be?
clarify.why: A few minutes of staleness allows TTL-only expiry. 'Must reflect writes within a second' needs explicit invalidation on every write, and handling of the races that come with it.

clarify.q: How big is the working set, and how big are typical and largest values?
clarify.why: Sets memory per shard and number of shards. A few multi-megabyte values can block a single-threaded shard and need limits.

clarify.q: What are the peak read and write rates, and the latency target?
clarify.why: For in-memory caches, operations per second usually decide the shard count before memory does.

clarify.q: Are there known hot keys, such as a homepage feed or a celebrity profile?
clarify.why: One key always lives on one shard. A key read 200 000 times a second needs special handling no matter how many shards we add.

clarify.q: Will many teams share one cluster?
clarify.why: Sharing needs namespaces, memory quotas and eviction that cannot let one team's traffic flush another team's data.
Each region needs its own cache. Invalidations then have to reach every region, or TTLs have to be short enough to bound the staleness.

functional: get, multi-get (up to 100 keys), set with TTL, delete, increment, and set-if-absent.
Compare-and-set and lease tokens, so a stale reader cannot overwrite a fresher value after an invalidation.
Namespaces per team, each with a memory quota, default TTL and eviction policy.
Add or remove shards and replace failed nodes without restarting clients.
Services can invalidate keys when the database changes, either directly or through a change-data-capture pipeline.
nonFunctional: Latency: p99 under 1 ms server-side and under 2 ms as seen by clients in the same zone.
Throughput: 1.5 M reads/s and 100 000 writes/s at peak now, 5× within two years.
Hit ratio of at least 95% on the main namespaces, because the databases are sized for 5% of reads.
Losing one node affects at most 1/20 of keys and fails over in under 10 seconds.
Bounded staleness: no value is served more than its TTL after the write that made it stale.
outOfScope: Using the cache as a primary data store (no durability guarantees).
Cross-region consistency beyond 'invalidations are broadcast; TTL bounds the rest'.
Querying or searching inside cached values.

assumptions: 1.5 M gets/s and 100 000 sets or deletes/s at peak
Working set: 500 M items; value about 1 KB, key about 60 B, about 140 B per-item overhead, so about 1.2 KB each
25% extra memory for fragmentation and headroom
One shard primary handles about 80 000 operations/s comfortably at 1 KB values (single-threaded command loop)
Databases behind the cache can take about 100 000 reads/s in total

steps.label: Shards by throughput
steps.result: 20 primaries; with one replica each, 40 nodes

steps.label: Shards by memory
steps.result: Fits on 64 GB machines. Throughput, not memory, sets the shard count

steps.label: One hot key
steps.math: 200 000 gets/s on one key vs 80 000 per shard; 200 000 × 1.1 KB = 220 MB/s ≈ 1.8 Gbit/s
steps.result: One key alone would need 2.5 shards' worth of CPU on a single shard

steps.label: Database load from misses
steps.result: A 15-point drop in hit ratio means 4× database load, 3× what the databases can take

steps.label: Rebalancing cost
steps.math: Adding shard 21 with hash mod N remaps 20/21 ≈ 95% of keys; with hash slots or consistent hashing ≈ 1/21 ≈ 4.8%
steps.result: mod N would empty the cache; slot moves keep about 95% of hits

estimates.takeaway: The cache is sized by operations per second: memory alone would allow 12 shards, but the CPU budget needs 20. The two numbers that should scare us are the hot key, at 2.5× a whole shard's capacity for one key, and the miss maths. The databases survive at a 95% hit ratio but get 4× their normal load at 80%. So most of the design is about protecting the hit ratio during failures, rebalancing and expiry storms, not about storing bytes.

api.note: On a miss, the first caller gets a lease token and is the one expected to fill the key. Callers within the next few seconds get 'miss, wait' and retry after 20 ms.

api.path: set(key, value, ttl, { leaseToken? | ifVersion? | nx? })
api.note: A set carrying a lease token is rejected if the key was deleted after the lease was issued, which closes the stale-fill race.
Also invalidates any outstanding lease for the key. Services call it after committing the database write.

api.returns: values[] in order, nulls for misses
api.note: The client library groups keys by shard and sends one request per shard in parallel.

api.body: { memoryGB, defaultTtlSec, eviction: lru | lfu, maxValueKB }
api.note: Admin API. Quotas stop one team's growth from evicting another team's data.

entities.name: Item
entities.store: In memory on the owning shard primary, replicated asynchronously to one replica
entities.why: Lookups by exact key only. All state is rebuildable from the databases, so there is no disk persistence on the hot path.

entities.name: SlotMap
entities.store: Cluster manager (backed by a small consensus store), cached in every client
entities.why: Lets clients route directly to the right shard in one hop. A client with an old map gets a redirect and refreshes.

entities.name: Namespace
entities.why: Per-team isolation and policy on a shared cluster.

data.note: Keys are prefixed with their namespace and an entity type, for example prof:user:42, so a whole namespace can be dropped by bumping a version in the prefix. 16 384 hash slots over 20 shards gives about 819 slots each. Moving slots one at a time with their data lets us rebalance without losing hits. To keep related keys on one shard for multi-key operations, wrap the shared part in a hash tag, {user:42}:profile.

hld.summary:
Services talk to the cache through a client library that holds the slot map. It routes each key straight to its shard, groups multi-gets by shard, runs a tiny in-process near cache for a short list of hot keys, and collapses concurrent misses for the same key into one fetch. The cache cluster is 20 shard primaries, each with a replica in another zone. A cluster manager watches health, promotes replicas when a primary dies, and moves slots during scaling.

The cache is cache-aside: on a miss the service reads the database and fills the cache. Writes go to the database first and then delete the key. A change-data-capture invalidator reads the database's change log and deletes affected keys too, as a safety net for code paths that forget, and for other regions.

diagram.title: Cache cluster with near cache and invalidation
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  S1["Service + cache client"] --> SH1["Shard 1 primary"]
  S1 --> SH2["Shard 2 primary"]
  S2["Service + cache client"] --> SH2
  S2 --> SH20["Shard 20 primary"]
  SH1 --> RP1["Shard 1 replica - other zone"]
  CM[Cluster manager] -. slot map and failover .-> S1
  CM -. health checks .-> SH1
  S1 --> DB[("Primary databases")]
  S2 --> DB
  DB --> CDC[Change log reader]
  CDC --> INV[Invalidator]
  INV --> SH2

flows.title: Read with a miss
steps: Client hashes the key to slot 7 210, which the slot map places on shard 9.
Shard 9 has no value. It returns a miss with lease token 881, and marks the lease as pending for 2 s.
Other requests for the same key in the next 2 s get 'miss, wait'. They retry after 20 ms, or serve a stale copy if the namespace allows it.
The lease holder reads the database (about 5 ms) and sets the value with token 881 and TTL 300 s ± 10%.
Waiting readers find the value on retry.

flows.title: Write path
steps: The service commits the database transaction.
It deletes the cache key (not an update), which also cancels any outstanding lease.
The CDC invalidator sees the same change in the database log within about 1 s and deletes the key again, in every region.
The next reader misses and fills the cache with the new value.

flows.title: A shard primary dies
steps: Cluster manager misses 3 health checks in a row (about 3 s) and confirms with a second observer.
It promotes the replica in the other zone and bumps the slot map epoch.
Clients that hit the dead node get connection errors, refresh the map and retry once. About 1/20 of keys see errors for under 10 s.
A new replica is created and synced from the new primary.

deepDives.title: Sharding and routing
deepDives.problem: Every request must find its shard in one hop. Adding or removing a shard must not wipe out the hit ratio, which by the earlier maths would quadruple database load. The routing logic also has to live somewhere: in each client, in a proxy, or in the servers.

options.name: Client-side consistent hashing
options.how: Each client has the server list and a hash ring with about 160 points per server. Changing servers moves only about 1/N of keys, and those keys simply miss.
pros: No extra hop, servers stay simple
Works with plain memcached-style servers
cons: Moved keys start empty, so adding a shard costs about 4.8% extra misses (72 000 DB reads/s here) until they refill
Every client in every language must agree on the hashing and the server list

options.name: Proxy tier
options.how: Clients talk to a fleet of stateless proxies that know the topology and forward requests to shards.
pros: Clients stay dumb, so any language works
Topology changes in one place, and proxies can pool connections, which matters with thousands of client processes
cons: An extra hop, about 0.2–0.5 ms, roughly doubling p50
Another fleet to scale (it carries all 1.6 M ops/s)

options.name: Hash slots with smart clients and redirects
options.how: Keys map to 16 384 fixed slots, and slots map to shards. Clients cache the slot map. A server that no longer owns a slot answers with a redirect to the new owner. Moving a slot copies its keys first.
pros: One hop
Rebalancing moves data with the slot, so hits are preserved
Failover is handled by the cluster, not by every client
cons: Multi-key operations only work within one slot (use hash tags)
Needs a capable client library in every language

deepDives.choice:
Hash slots with smart clients, because protecting the hit ratio during scaling is the top concern, and moving slots with their data keeps about 95% of hits during a rebalance. Add a proxy tier only for languages without a good client, and for serverless callers that would otherwise open thousands of short connections.

What would change my mind: a pure memcached deployment, where client-side consistent hashing is the norm. Then I would add shards gradually, at off-peak times, one at a time, and pre-warm each new shard from a key list.

deepDives.title: Hot keys
deepDives.problem: A key always lives on one shard. The homepage config or a celebrity profile at 200 000 gets/s needs 2.5× one shard's CPU and about 1.8 Gbit/s of network on one machine. Adding shards does nothing for it.

options.name: Near cache in the client
options.how: The client library keeps hot keys in process memory for 1–5 s. Hot keys are found by sampling access counts in the client, or from a list the shards publish.
pros: Removes nearly all traffic for the key: with 500 client processes and a 2 s TTL, the shard sees about 250 gets/s instead of 200 000
No server changes
cons: Up to 2 s of extra staleness for those keys, and deletes do not reach process memory unless broadcast
Uses memory in every process

options.name: Replicate the key under several names
options.how: Write the value to key#0 … key#7, which land in different slots. Readers pick a random suffix, and writers update or delete all copies.
pros: Spreads one key over 8 shards
Keeps server-side freshness
cons: Writes and deletes cost 8×, and a partial failure leaves copies out of step
Callers must know which keys are hot

options.name: Read from replicas
options.how: Allow reads for hot slots from the replica too.
pros: Doubles capacity for that slot with no client tricks
cons: Only 2×, which is not enough here
Replicas lag slightly (asynchronous replication)

deepDives.choice:
Near cache with a short TTL for detected hot keys, because it solves the 200 000/s case by a factor of about 800 with no change to the servers. Detection runs in the client: it samples 1% of gets and promotes keys above 1 000 gets/s per process. Namespaces that cannot tolerate 2 s of extra staleness opt out and use key replication for a known short list.

What would change my mind: if the hot keys are writes (counters, likes), none of this helps. Then shard the counter itself into N sub-counters and sum them on read.

deepDives.title: Stampedes when a hot key expires
deepDives.problem: A key read 20 000 times a second expires. The database query to rebuild it takes 50 ms. In those 50 ms about 20 000 × 0.05 = 1 000 requests miss and all go to the database for the same row. Across many keys expiring together (a deploy, a TTL set at the same moment), this can take the database down.

options.name: Lease or lock on miss
options.how: The first miss gets a lease to fill the key; everyone else waits briefly or gets a stale value. The client library also collapses concurrent misses inside one process.
pros: Exactly one database query per key per expiry
Also closes the stale-fill race (see consistency)
cons: Waiters add latency (a few retries of 20 ms)
If the lease holder dies, others wait for the lease timeout (2 s)

options.name: Refresh before expiry, at random
options.how: Each read, if the key is close to expiry, has a small chance to refresh it in the background. The chance rises as expiry nears and with how long the rebuild takes.
pros: Hot keys rarely expire at all
No coordination
cons: Some duplicate refreshes
Does nothing for cold keys or for a cache that just restarted

options.name: Serve stale while revalidating
options.how: Store a soft TTL inside the value and a longer hard TTL on the key. After the soft TTL, serve the old value and trigger one refresh.
pros: Readers never wait
The database sees one refresh per key
cons: Readers see data older than the soft TTL
Needs the value format to carry a timestamp

options.name: TTL jitter
options.how: Add ±10% random jitter to every TTL.
pros: Stops keys written together from expiring together
One line of code
cons: Does nothing for one hot key

deepDives.choice:
All of them, layered. TTL jitter everywhere. Leases on every miss, so the database sees one query per key. Stale-while-revalidate for namespaces that accept it, which most read models do. In-process request collapsing in the client, so each of the 500 processes sends at most one lease request per key, however many of its own requests are waiting.

For a full cold start (whole cluster restarted), leases are not enough, because every key misses at once. Clients then rate-limit misses per namespace (for example 20 000 DB reads/s) and fail fast or serve defaults beyond that, while a warmer job pre-loads the top 1 M keys from yesterday's access log.

What would change my mind: a namespace where stale data is never acceptable (prices at checkout) does not use stale-while-revalidate. It should be read from the database or kept fresh by write-through.

deepDives.title: Eviction and memory
deepDives.problem: A shared cluster will be full, so something is always being evicted. A bad policy lets one team's batch job, scanning millions of keys once, flush everybody's hot data. Large values fragment memory, and a 10 MB value blocks a single-threaded shard for milliseconds.

options.name: Approximate LRU
options.how: On memory pressure, sample a few keys and evict the least recently used among them.
pros: Cheap, no linked list per item
Good for recency-heavy workloads
cons: A one-off scan of cold keys pushes out genuinely hot ones

options.name: Approximate LFU with decay
options.how: Keep a small logarithmic access counter per key that decays over time, and evict the lowest counts.
pros: Resists scans: a key touched once ranks below one touched 1 000 times
Decay lets yesterday's hot keys fade
cons: New keys start with low counts and can be evicted before they prove themselves
Two tuning knobs (log factor, decay time)

options.name: Hard quotas per namespace
options.how: Each namespace has a memory limit and evicts only its own keys, enforced on each shard as quota / shard count.
pros: One team cannot hurt another
Makes capacity a per-team budget
cons: Unused quota is wasted unless we allow borrowing
Uneven key spread can trip per-shard limits early

deepDives.choice:
Namespace quotas plus approximate LFU inside each namespace, with the option of LRU for namespaces whose access pattern is mostly recency. Every key has a TTL (default 1 h, maximum 7 days), so abandoned data ages out without eviction. Values are capped at 512 KB by default. A value over 1 MB is usually a design bug, and serving it blocks the shard for about a millisecond.

What would change my mind: a single-purpose cluster for one service with a known working set that fits in memory. Then plain LRU and no quotas is simpler.

deepDives.title: Keeping the cache consistent with the database
deepDives.problem: Cache-aside has a classic race. A reader misses and loads v1 from the database. A writer commits v2 and deletes the key. Then the slow reader writes v1 into the cache. The cache now holds stale data until its TTL, possibly an hour, even though every step looked correct.

options.name: Delete after write, rely on TTL
options.how: Commit to the database, then delete the key. The TTL bounds any race.
pros: Simple and widely understood
cons: The race above leaves stale data for up to the TTL
If the delete fails (crash after commit), staleness also lasts up to the TTL

options.name: Write-through
options.how: The write path updates the database and then sets the new value in the cache.
pros: Fresh value is cached immediately, no miss after a write
cons: Two concurrent writers can set the cache in the opposite order from the database commits
Caches values nobody may read

options.name: Leases or versioned sets
options.how: A miss returns a lease. A delete cancels all leases for that key, so the slow reader's set with the old lease is rejected. Alternatively, store the database row version and only accept a set with a higher version.
pros: Closes the race rather than bounding it
Works with the stampede protection we already need
cons: Requires lease or compare-and-set support in the server and the client
Lease bookkeeping costs a little memory

options.name: Invalidate from the database change log
options.how: A consumer reads the change-data-capture stream and deletes affected keys, independently of application code.
pros: Catches writes from every code path, scripts and migrations included
Natural way to reach other regions
cons: Adds about 1 s of lag
Needs a mapping from table rows to cache keys

deepDives.choice:
Delete after commit, plus leases, plus change-log invalidation as a backstop. Leases close the reader-writer race. The change-log invalidator catches crashed deletes and writes from other services, and handles other regions. The TTL is the last line, bounding anything all three miss.

What would change my mind: data where no staleness is acceptable at all. Then it should not be served from a cache at read time. Read from the database primary, or make the cache part of the write transaction's ownership (a single service owning both).

diagram.title: The stale-fill race and how a lease stops it
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as Reader
  participant C as Cache
  participant D as Database
  participant W as Writer
  R->>C: get user 42
  C-->>R: miss with lease 881
  R->>D: select user 42
  D-->>R: v1
  W->>D: update user 42 to v2
  W->>C: delete user 42
  Note over C: lease 881 is cancelled
  R->>C: set v1 with lease 881
  C-->>R: rejected
  Note over C: next reader loads v2

failures: Replica in another zone is promoted in under 10 s. About 1/20 of keys error or miss briefly. Asynchronous replication may lose the last few ms of sets, which only cost misses.
Clients cap database reads per namespace (for example 20 000/s) and serve defaults or errors beyond that. A warmer pre-loads the top 1 M keys. Gradually raise the cap as the hit ratio recovers.
A team stores 8 MB values and shard latency jumps
Enforce maxValueKB per namespace at the client and the server. Alert on large-value writes and on slow commands. Move big blobs to object storage and cache a pointer instead.
The invalidation pipeline lags by 10 minutes
Direct deletes from the write path still work. Alert on consumer lag above 30 s. TTLs bound the worst case. For sensitive namespaces, shorten TTLs automatically while lag is high.
A client fleet ships with an old slot map after a rebalance
Servers answer with redirects, clients refresh the map on the first redirect. A bug that ignores redirects shows up as a redirect-rate alert, not as wrong data.
Network partition between one zone's services and a shard
Client timeout of 5 ms and a circuit breaker per shard. Treat that shard as a miss, protected by the per-namespace database read cap, instead of waiting on it.
scale: 5× (8 M ops/s): about 100 primaries. Cluster gossip and failover still cope at this size, but beyond a few hundred nodes split into several clusters by namespace group, each with its own slot map.
Hot-key share grows: the near cache carries more of the load. Make hot-key detection server-assisted, with shards publishing their top keys every second.
Multiple regions: one cluster per region, never read across regions. Change-log invalidations fan out to every region, and TTLs are shortened for data that changes often.

followups.q: Why delete the key on write instead of setting the new value?
answer: Two writers can commit v2 then v3 in the database but set the cache in the order v3 then v2, leaving v2 cached. Deletes in any order leave the key empty, which is safe.
A delete does not waste memory on values nobody reads.
The cost is one miss after each write, which leases make cheap.
Memcached is multi-threaded, so it handles more ops per node for plain gets and sets, and it is simpler to run.
Redis offers data structures, scripts, replication and cluster slot migration, which we used for leases, failover and rebalancing without losing hits.
For a shared platform with these features, Redis-style clusters; for a single pure key-value workload at very high ops per node, Memcached is a fine choice.
Yes, briefly: repeated lookups of missing ids (bots, typos) otherwise all reach the database.
Store a small 'missing' marker with a short TTL, for example 30 s, so a newly created row appears quickly.
Delete the marker on create, through the same invalidation path.

followups.q: How would you pick the TTL for a namespace?
answer: Start from tolerated staleness: the TTL is the worst case if every invalidation fails.
Check the hit ratio curve. If doubling the TTL barely raises hits, keep it short.
Watch memory: items × size must fit the quota. Long TTLs on rarely read data only add eviction pressure.

followups.q: How do you know the cache is helping and healthy?
answer: Hit ratio per namespace, database reads per second caused by misses, and p99 latency per shard.
Eviction rate and memory per namespace, against quota.
Hot keys per shard and the near cache's share of reads.

mistakes: Sizing shards by memory only, ending with 12 shards that run out of CPU at 130 000 ops/s each.
Using hash mod N for routing, so adding one node empties about 95% of the cache.
Saying 'add more shards' for a hot key, which always lives on one shard.
Ignoring the stale-fill race in cache-aside, or claiming write-through is always consistent.
Forgetting that a cold or failed cache multiplies database load, with no plan to cap misses.

Gave every key a TTL and named an eviction policy
senior: Quantified a hot key against one shard's capacity and proposed a near cache or key replication
Described the stampede maths (requests × rebuild time) and fixed it with leases or request collapsing
Showed the cache-aside race with a timeline and closed it with leases or versions
Planned failover with replicas in another zone and gave a recovery time
Computed database load at different hit ratios
staff: Designed multi-tenancy: namespaces, quotas and eviction that one team cannot abuse
Planned for a full cold start with database read caps and a warmer
Added change-log invalidation as a backstop and covered multi-region invalidation
